new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress in Turoyo is on the penultimate syllable (contrast: final in the sister language Mlaḥsô). Stress stays penultimate when nominal suffixes are added (ṭúro > ṭuróne). In verb forms built on the old participle bases, stress may not move rightward past the participle base no matter how many suffixes/enclitics follow, so long suffixed verb forms surface with antepenultimate or earlier stress; stress is thereby contrastive at the morphological level (malim 'he collects' vs 'collect!' differ only in stress). Proclitic article, numerals and negation form stress groups with the following word in which the main stress sits on the (last syllable of the) first element (ló=xile 'he did not eat'; JAAS: ú-bayto 'the house', ák-karme 'the vineyards'). Talay 2017 states the same rule independently: 'In Surayt as a rule the penultimate syllable in the word is stressed'; 'the definite article is always stressed: gáwro but ú-gawro'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described by Jastrow 1997 or Talay 2017. Prym & Socin 1881 mark 'Haupt- oder Nebenaccent' in their texts and say a word that loses main stress to a clitic keeps a Nebenton, but give no rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Deviations from penultimate are marked with an accent in Jastrow's transcription; systematic non-penultimate cases: (i) suffixed verb forms on participle bases (stress frozen on the base), (ii) morphologically contrastive final stress in some verb forms (malim 'he collects' vs imperative), (iii) stress groups where article/numeral/negation take the main stress (ú-gawro, tlóṯo=.., ló=xile), (iv) special stressed L-suffix endings in the verb ʾzl 'go' (əzzé, azzí; Noorlander in Khan & Noorlander 2021: 49). Midyat town dialect additionally shortens long vowels in pretonic open syllables (Jastrow JAAS p.14), which presupposes the same stress placement.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated for citation forms; the definite article and other proclitics form a single stress unit ('stress group', Talay: 'Toneinheit') with the host and carry its main stress, so the phonological word for stress includes the article. Jastrow's data: Mīdin village and Midyat; Talay: unified diaspora Surayt.
new_statements.identity_note: Jastrow's Turoyo data (1997 chapter, JAAS article) rest on his fieldwork on the village dialect of Mīdin and on Midyat town Turoyo; he notes Midyat differs from the villages only in pretonic vowel shortening, not in stress placement. Talay 2017 explicitly teaches a 'slightly unified' diaspora Surayt rather than any single Tur Abdin local dialect. Both fall under Glottolog turo1239 (no sub-dialect glottocodes needed); Mlaḥsô (mlah1239), the sister language, is contrasted as having final stress.

sources.note: p.350: word stress falls on the last syllable in Mlaḥsô but on the second-to-last in Ṭuroyo; p.353 'Word Stress': stress shifted to the penultimate (Ṭuroyo gawro 'man', ḥoze 'he sees'); penultimate also under suffixation (ṭuro/ṭurone); in verb forms built on old participles stress cannot move beyond the participle however many suffixes follow (ḥozeno, ḥozenole, ḥozewaynole); stress phonemic on the morphological level (malim 'he collects' vs malim 'collect!'); 'Stress Groups': article/numeral/negation + word, main stress on last syllable of first word (Ṭuroyo lo=xile, tloṯo=naqlawoṯe).

sources.note: Lesson 2.4 sec. 4 'Placement of stress': 'In Surayt as a rule the penultimate (second to the last) syllable in the word is stressed. The article works together with the noun.. thereby it carries the main tone.' (German: 'Im Surayt wird in der Regel die vorletzte Silbe im Wort betont. Der Artikel bildet mit dem zugehörigen Substantiv eine Toneinheit, dabei trägt er den Hauptton.') Lesson 3.3a: 'The definite article is always stressed..: gáwro but ú-gawro; áṯto but í-aṯto; nóše but án-noše.'
